soil-bio-292.title: Why roots build more soil organic matter than shoots
soil-bio-292.text: Roots are probably the most effective way to raise soil organic matter. Weight for weight, they add a larger share to persistent organic matter than aboveground residues do. They are well distributed, in close contact with soil, and often richer in slowly decomposing {{ref:soil-bio-116}} than aboveground parts. In an oat experiment one-third of surface residue remained after a year, but 42% of root organic matter did. For hairy vetch, 13% of aboveground carbon and nearly 50% of root carbon remained after five months. Root residue also contributed much more to {{ref:soil-bio-118}} than aboveground residue. Roots decompose more slowly, add more to stable organic matter, and need no incorporation to reach depth.

soil-bio-287.title: How organic matter shapes the water cycle
soil-bio-287.text: Organic matter works on water from the field scale up to the global one. Soils rich in it, with good tilth, let rainwater infiltrate quickly and store more of it. The water may serve plants or percolate down to recharge groundwater. When organic matter is depleted, the soil accepts and stores less water. Runoff and erosion rise, and plants and groundwater recharge get less.

soil-bio-319.title: Converting organic matter to carbon, and its weakness
soil-bio-319.text: Soil organic carbon and soil organic matter are different quantities. They are routinely converted by assuming that carbon is 58% of organic matter mass, a factor of 1.72. That figure comes from Waksman and Stevens (1930), who urged caution. Organic matter also holds hydrogen (about 4%) and oxygen (about 30%), and these vary with the state of decomposition. Reviews of many studies find that actual factors are usually higher than 1.72, meaning carbon is a smaller share of organic matter. The best approach is separate direct analyses. Otherwise, state what was analyzed and how values were converted.

soil-bio-288.title: Why clay soils hold more organic matter than sand
soil-bio-288.text: Organic matter is under 1% in sands, 2-3% in loams, and 4% to over 5% in clays. Fine-textured soils hold more for three reasons. Strong bonds between organic matter and clay or fine silt protect molecules from microbes and enzymes. Tiny aggregates shield organic matter inside them. Smaller pores and less oxygen in fine soils further limit decomposition. See {{ref:soil-found-051}} and {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-290.title: Why grassland soils are richer than forest soils
soil-bio-290.text: Soils formed under grassland hold more organic matter, distributed deeper, than soils formed under forest. Grassland roots are deep, extensive and turn over quickly. Slow grass fires also add biochar that resists degradation. This helps explain why former grassland soils are highly productive. Forests do it differently. Litter piles on the surface, where organic layers often exceed 50% organic matter, but the mineral layers beneath usually contain less than 2%. The root effect is strong in crops too: about 25-40% of a perennial wheatgrass root system dies back each year, adding much more organic matter than annual wheat. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-318.title: The Walkley-Black method and its biases
soil-bio-318.text: The Walkley-Black method oxidizes organic carbon with chromate, heated by added sulfuric acid, and titrates the leftover chromate to get the carbon. It was once the standard method. It oxidizes carbon incompletely, so a correction factor that varies with soil type is needed, and this biases the results. Carbon present as charcoal may be missed, which underestimates total soil carbon.

soil-bio-324.title: Isotope-ratio mass spectrometry: weighing atoms by type
soil-bio-324.text:
Isotope-ratio mass spectrometry measures the relative abundance of isotopes in a sample. It serves both stable-isotope and radiogenic-isotope studies. Stable-isotope analysis measures variations from mass-dependent fractionation, while radiogenic analysis measures decay products and underpins most long-lived radiometric dating.

Magnetic sector instruments are preferred over quadrupoles because they allow multiple-collector analysis and give good peak shapes. Ions are accelerated, bent by mass-to-charge ratio and counted in Faraday cups. Light elements such as H, C and O are measured as pure gases from combustion, GC or chemical trapping, against standards: carbon uses VPDB and oxygen uses V-SMOW.

Thermal ionization MS suits low-ionization elements like Sr and Pb. MC-ICP-MS reaches elements such as Hf-W and Lu-Hf that TIMS cannot. Quadrupole ICP-MS precision is only about 1%.

soil-bio-325.title: Accelerator mass spectrometry for very rare isotopes
soil-bio-325.text: Some isotopes are so rare that ordinary instruments cannot count them. Accelerator mass spectrometry is an isotope-ratio technique for such extremely low levels, and it accelerates negative ions through a mega-volt potential. Charge exchange removes interfering species, and energy-loss detectors separate ions of the same mass-to-charge ratio. This allows isotope ratios above 10^12. It extended 14C dating to about 60,000 years BP and is about 10^6 times more sensitive than conventional IRMS. It builds on {{ref:soil-bio-324}}.

soil-bio-323.title: Isotope dilution: measuring by adding a known spike
soil-bio-323.text:
Isotope dilution measures how much of a substance a sample holds by adding a known amount of an isotopically enriched form of it. The enriched standard dilutes the sample's isotopic composition. The method works from signal ratios, not intensities, and is an internal standardisation method, which gives it very high metrological standing. It is almost always paired with mass spectrometry. National metrology institutes use it to certify reference materials, and it helps when analyte recovery is low.

The gains are measurable. In gas chromatography it can cut uncertainty from 5% to 1%, and isotope dilution mass spectrometry measures ratios to better than 0.25%. Double (reverse) dilution first calibrates the enriched spike against a natural-composition standard, because spikes come in small amounts of questionable purity. The principle is analogous to mark-and-recapture population estimates in ecology.

soil-class-006.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series
soil-class-006.text:
The United States sorts its soils into 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series. USDA soil taxonomy is the classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the National Cooperative Soil Survey. It sorts soils by their properties into six levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series. The lab manual describes it as a quantitative hierarchy running from 12 broad orders to more than 23,000 series, and says it helps carry management research between similar soils worldwide. Sources differ on the series count: the more than 14,000 above is the United States figure.

It uses properties that can be measured: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content. It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and soil management, and it supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units. Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed. It builds on {{ref:soil-class-001}}, {{ref:soil-class-005}}, {{ref:soil-found-001}} and {{ref:soil-form-017}}.

Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system. Work began by 1945. A series of approximations followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.

soil-class-025.title: Canadian Organic soils: the peatland order
soil-class-025.text:
Organic soils cover almost 374,000 km2 (4.1%) of Canada, with large areas in Manitoba, Ontario and northern Alberta. They are the Canadian order of soils made mostly of organic matter, over 30% by weight in the upper half metre, without permafrost near the surface. They are the main soils of peatlands such as swamps, bogs and fens, mostly built from plants of waterlogged ground. Some come from lake deposits or forest litter on rainy, rocky slopes.

Four great groups follow decomposition. Little-decomposed soils with over 40% fibre, mostly from Sphagnum, are Fibrisols. Others have 10-40% or up to 10% fibre, and a fourth group is thick forest-litter soils over rock. Wetland soils with an O horizon at least 40 cm thick are Organic. With less than 40 cm or none they are Gleysolic. See {{ref:soil-class-023}}, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and {{ref:soil-bio-114}}.

soil-class-165.title: Working through the Keys to Soil Taxonomy
soil-class-165.text: To classify a soil, work through the Keys to Soil Taxonomy, starting with the key to soil orders and eliminating classes whose criteria the soil fails. The first order whose criteria the soil meets is chosen, and the same process runs through suborder, great group and subgroup. Family and series use other criteria in the Keys. Suborders rest on soil moisture regimes and diagnostic features. Great groups rest on how strongly diagnostic horizons are expressed. Subgroups rest on properties transitional to other orders, suborders and great groups. The family name combines terms such as particle size class, mineralogy of the control section, soil temperature regime, CEC and depth. The levels themselves are set out in {{ref:soil-class-006}}.

soil-class-164.title: Describing a soil profile, step by step
soil-class-164.text: A profile description records each horizon's depth, color, texture, structure, consistence, roots, pH and boundary, so one soil can be told from another. The steps are: observe the landscape setting, examine morphology to separate horizons, describe each horizon in detail, assign horizon designations, then classify the soil by its morphology and horizonation. In the Harney silt loam example, the Ap horizon is 0 to 9 in, dark grayish brown (Munsell 10YR 4/2), silt loam, with moderate medium granular structure, very friable, many fine roots and slightly acid. Classification then reads the names. Formative elements give each level a connotation, and the bolded syllable of each order name appears in the names of its suborders and lower levels. In the Clarion-Nicollet-Webster-Glencoe catena, the wetter the drainage class the more the 'aqu' element appears, because Soil Taxonomy prioritizes management concerns such as a shallow water table. See {{ref:soil-form-004}} and {{ref:soil-class-165}}.

soil-class-166.title: Canadian soil classification, level by level
soil-class-166.text: In the Canadian System of Soil Classification each pedon fits only one class, assigned by comparing its horizons with diagnostic properties. Orders reflect the overall soil environment and the dominant soil-forming process. Great groups reflect differences in the strength of those processes, or a major added process. Subgroups differ by closeness to the central (Orthic) concept, transition toward another order and special features. Families group series of one subgroup with similar management and engineering response, but are seldom used in Canada. A profile is assigned its class by comparing its field horizons with a list of diagnostic properties. A related land rating covered about 2.6 million km2, about 25% of Canada's land mass, and rated each area in 7 classes by its most severe limitation, with classes 1 to 3 the prime lands. Compare {{ref:soil-class-001}}.

soil-class-167.title: Dry quicksand: sand that swallows without water
soil-class-167.text:
Quicksand without water was long doubted as folklore. It was created in the laboratory in 2004, though its prevalence in nature is unclear. Dry quicksand is loose sand whose bulk density has been lowered by blowing air through it, so it gives way easily under weight or pressure. It behaves like ordinary {{ref:soil-phys-118}} but contains no water and works on a different principle. It can also result from contractive dilatancy.

In Lohse's experiment, fine sand with grains about 40 micrometers, with air blown through it, settled to a packing fraction of only 41%, against 55-60% for untreated {{ref:soil-phys-014}}. A weighted table tennis ball dropped on it sank about five diameters, and a jet of sand shot upward after about 100 ms. In nature it might form when very fine blown sand settles.

soil-fert-184.title: The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio: why some residues starve plants
soil-fert-184.text:
Mix redwood sawdust into a garden and the plants may go hungry. Sawdust runs about 1020:1 in one list and 250 in another, while bacteria are only 4. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is the ratio of the mass of carbon to the mass of nitrogen in organic residues. In soil it expresses the balance between energy food for microbes, represented by carbon, and protein-building material, represented by nitrogen. See {{ref:soil-fert-172}}.

Plant residues typically run from 13:1 to 100:1, from alfalfa at 13 to oat straw at 80. A second list gives microorganisms 8:1, clover hay 20:1, barnyard manure 25:1, corn stalks 73:1 and barley straw 450:1. Microbes themselves are about 10:1. A ratio around 24:1 gives high microbial activity, and 30:1 is recommended for soil materials.

Above 30:1, residues leave microbes short of nitrogen, so they take up soil ammonium and nitrate and immobilize them. Below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants. Excess carbon makes microbes compete with plants for soil nitrogen until the microbes die. Excess nitrogen is left behind but may be leached.

As microbes and soil fauna digest organic matter and release CO2, the ratio falls, and a lower soil ratio correlates with higher productivity. Compost, manure and mulch can modify a soil's ratio, and a soil test can measure it. Related: {{ref:soil-found-045}} and {{ref:soil-found-048}}.
